transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Um… mostly I’m having trouble staying on track. Like, I’ll try to work on an application or something, and then some little noise outside, my phone, or just a random thought pulls me away. I don’t always notice it happening until I’m already doing something else.
Did you have this same kind of trouble paying attention when you were a child?

Yeah… I think so. Even back in elementary school, teachers would move my seat around because I talked too much or blurted things out. I’d forget homework a lot, too, and rush through worksheets and make dumb mistakes.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually energetic or wired for several days in a row?
Um… I don’t think so. I mean, I get restless or keyed up sometimes, but not like several days where I’m unusually wired or anything.
Do these focus problems cause trouble in more than one part of your life, like both at work or school and at home?

Yeah… it’s not just one place. Like, with the training stuff and applications for automotive work, I keep missing deadlines or having to redo things. So I’m kind of stuck, even though I think I’d be fine with the hands-on part.
When you’re trying to focus, do you often find that worry is what pulls your attention away?
I don’t know… not usually, I guess. Sometimes I worry, but I wouldn’t say that’s the main thing pulling me off task.
Do you often feel fidgety or like you have trouble sitting still?
Yeah… I guess so. If I’m sitting with someone, my leg’s usually bouncing or I’m clicking a pen, messing with my keys… half the time I don’t even notice I’m doing it.
Have you been losing interest in things you usually enjoy?
Not really… I mean, I still like the same stuff. I just don’t always get around to doing it, I guess.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset and current persistence across settings. Confirmed symptoms include distractibility, careless mistakes, forgetfulness, blurting/talking excessively, and fidgetiness/restlessness, causing occupational/academic impairment. Bipolar and depressive syndromes were not supported, and worry was not the primary driver of inattention.
